candidate_relations.reason: Presumed UTI was the first-pass diagnosis and does not explain the expanding popliteal aneurysm and thigh hematoma.
Ruptured popliteal artery aneurysm matches the CTA saccular popliteal aneurysm with a large posterior thigh collection and falling hemoglobin.
Venous thromboembolism was considered and excluded by Wells score and a patent venous ultrasound.
Normocytic then worsening anemia is a hemorrhagic manifestation of aneurysm rupture, not the vascular diagnosis.
Atherosclerosis is reflected in diseased but patent runoff vessels, not the ruptured aneurysm itself.
The medial/posterior thigh hematoma is the hemorrhage from rupture rather than the aneurysm diagnosis.
The foot was pulseless without signs of acute ischemia, so acute limb ischemia is not the diagnosis.
Deep vein thrombosis was the suspected cause of swelling but ultrasound showed a patent venous system.
Collapse and hemoglobin drop reflect blood loss from rupture rather than a standalone hemorrhagic-shock diagnosis.
Chronically diseased runoff without acute ischemic signs is associated vascular disease, not the rupture.
Popliteal artery aneurysm is the parent lesion but omits the required rupture with expanding hematoma.
Arterial thromboembolism is a different mechanism from aneurysmal rupture with hematoma.
Antiphospholipid syndrome is not supported and is a different entity from ruptured popliteal aneurysm.
Vasculitis is a different vascular disease and is not indicated by the saccular popliteal aneurysm.
